overview: The Eastern Zhou saw the Zhou kings reduced to figureheads while rival states competed for power. This political fragmentation paradoxically produced China's greatest intellectual flowering, as philosophers offered competing visions of the good society.

items.text: Confucius born in the state of Lu; he teaches ethics, proper conduct and the restoration of Zhou ritual.
Mozi advocates universal love and utilitarian ethics as alternatives to Confucianism.

The Daodejing, attributed to the sage Laozi, is in circulation by about 300 BCE, the date of the earliest copies found in a tomb at Guodian; it founds the Daoist philosophy of naturalness and non-action.
Mencius develops Confucian ideas of innate human goodness and the right to rebel against unjust rulers.
Cast iron production begins, allowing mass production of agricultural tools.
Crossbows with bronze trigger mechanisms appear in warfare.
Iron tools replace stone and bronze in agriculture and crafts.
The Spring and Autumn Annals compiled in Lu, the first Chinese chronicle history, covering 722 to 481 BCE.
The Zuozhuan and other commentaries elaborate on historical events with narrative detail.
Lacquerware production reaches new heights of craftsmanship, above all in the southern state of Chu.
Walled cities grow as commercial centers with specialized crafts and markets.
Coinage in bronze spade and knife shapes facilitates trade between states.
Professional bureaucrats and scholars travel between courts seeking employment.
Trade networks connect the Yellow River states with the Yangzi valley and the southern coast.
Salt and iron become major commodities in interstate commerce.
The Hundred Schools of Thought established the major philosophical traditions of East Asia.
Military innovations and statecraft from this period influenced later imperial administration.
The concept of a unified Chinese cultural sphere emerged despite political division.

fall.text: The Qin state conquered the last Zhou territories in 256 BCE, and the last Zhou king died that year, ending the dynasty.

sources.title: Michael Loewe and Edward L. Shaughnessy (eds.), The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999), chapters 7 to 11
